paras.text: MIOSHA Construction Safety — Audio Lecture

This chapter covers MIOSHA construction safety, which is worth about ten of the one hundred ten trade questions on your Michigan Residential Builder exam. That's ten questions you can lock down almost entirely with memorized numbers, because safety questions are number questions. Heights, depths, hours, dollar amounts. If you know the numbers cold, this is the easiest section on the whole test. Let's get them into your head.

Start with the big picture. MIOSHA stands for the Michigan Occupational Safety and Health Administration. It was created by the MIOSHA Act, which is Act one fifty four of nineteen seventy four. Michigan runs its own state plan, which by federal law must be at least as effective as federal OSHA. And here's a favorite exam discriminator: MIOSHA covers public sector employees, meaning state, county, and city workers, while federal OSHA does not. If a question asks who MIOSHA protects that federal OSHA doesn't, the answer is public employees.

Who runs MIOSHA today? The Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity, L E O. Not LARA. It moved from LARA to L E O by executive order back in twenty nineteen. On construction sites, the enforcement arm is the Construction Safety and Health Division. If an answer choice says LARA administers MIOSHA, that's the trap.

Next, the General Duty Clause. Every employer must furnish a workplace free from recognized hazards that are causing or likely to cause death or serious physical harm. That's M C L four oh eight point ten eleven. The key idea: it applies when no specific standard covers the hazard. It's the catch-all. And under the construction general rules, every construction employer must also have an accident prevention program. Not optional, even for a small crew.
Now the site rules, and we'll go part by part.

Fall protection is Part forty five. The trigger is six feet. If a work area is six feet or more above a lower level, workers need fall protection. Three conventional systems: guardrails, safety nets, or a personal fall arrest system, meaning harness, lanyard, and anchorage. A guardrail top rail sits at forty two inches, plus or minus three, and must take a two hundred pound force. In a personal fall arrest system, maximum free fall is six feet, and the rig can't let the worker hit a lower level. The anchorage must hold five thousand pounds per worker. On a residential roof where conventional systems are truly infeasible at a particular spot, the fallback is a written, site-specific fall protection plan.

Ladders are Part eleven. Four numbers. First, the angle: four to one. For every four feet of height, the base sits one foot out. Second, the extension: side rails must extend at least three feet above the upper landing. So a ladder to a sixteen foot eave needs to reach about nineteen feet, with the base about four feet out. Third: secure it. Safety feet, or tie it, block it, or otherwise fix it in place. And never stand on the top three feet. One more Part eleven surprise that trips people: a portable ladder near power transmission or distribution lines needs twenty feet of clearance. Twenty for ladders. That's different from the ten foot clearance for equipment near lines up to fifty kilovolts. Ladders twenty, equipment ten.

Scaffolds are Part twelve, and here lives the single most-tested trap in this whole domain. General fall protection triggers at six feet. But a guardrail on the open side of a scaffold platform is required at ten feet. Read the question. If it says scaffold, the answer is ten. If it says leading edge, floor opening, or just general fall protection, the answer is six. Other scaffold numbers: a scaffold must support four times its maximum intended load. Planking is scaffold grade two by ten. Access must be a ladder, stair, or ramp, and climbing the cross braces is always a violation. Suspension type scaffolds, like a boatswain's chair or ladder jack, require a personal fall arrest system, and a two-point suspension scaffold requires both a harness system and a guardrail.

Excavation is Part nine, and it's dense with numbers, so slow down here. A trench or excavation more than five feet deep requires a protective system: sloping, shoring, or a trench shield. Below five feet you still need protection if the ground shows signs of hazardous movement. Egress is a separate rule with a separate number: at four feet deep, forty eight inches, workers need a ladder, and that ladder must extend three feet above the top of the trench and be within twenty five feet of lateral travel of every worker. So four feet means ladder, five feet means protective system. Don't let the exam swap those. Spoil piles and equipment stay at least two feet back from the edge. And a competent person, someone who can spot hazards and has authority to fix them, must inspect the excavation on an ongoing basis and again after every rainstorm.

Soil types. The exam tests the federal three-letter system. Type A is the most stable: clay, silty clay. Maximum slope three quarters horizontal to one vertical, which is fifty three degrees. Type B is the middle: silt, angular gravel, and any previously disturbed soil. Slope one to one, forty five degrees. Type C is the weakest: sand, gravel, anything submerged or seeping water. Slope one and a half horizontal to one vertical, thirty four degrees, the flattest slope. Two memory hooks. The weaker the soil, the flatter the slope. And previously disturbed soil can never be Type A, so around existing utilities you're at Type B at best.

Before any of that digging, Michigan law says contact MISS DIG eight one one at least three full working days before you excavate. Know the colors: red is electric, yellow is gas or oil, orange is telecom, blue is water, green is sewer, white marks your proposed dig, pink is survey, purple is reclaimed water.

Electrical is Part seventeen. Every one hundred twenty volt, fifteen or twenty amp receptacle that isn't part of the building's permanent wiring needs G F C I protection. The alternative is an assured equipment grounding conductor program, a documented testing program covering every cord set, temporary receptacle, and plug-connected tool. G F C I or the assured grounding program, one or the other. And lockout tagout: before servicing equipment, de-energize it, lock it, and tag it.

A few health and P P E items. First aid: a person with a valid first aid certificate must be present at the worksite. Silica: the permissible exposure limit is fifty micrograms per cubic meter over eight hours, and the action level is twenty five. Wet cutting and vacuum collection come before respirators. Noise: in construction the limit is ninety decibels over eight hours. The eighty five decibel action level with hearing tests is a general industry rule, not construction, and yes, they will bait you with eighty five. Hazard communication is the right to know: labels, safety data sheets, and training. A safety data sheet must be on site and accessible for every hazardous chemical, no matter who brought it. Confined spaces: big enough to enter, limited entry and exit, not designed for occupancy, and you test the atmosphere before anyone goes in.

Now enforcement, because a builder is an employer. A MIOSHA inspector who shows credentials may enter your site without delay at reasonable times. No advance notice, and tipping off an employer is itself an offense. You can insist on a warrant, but they'll get one. The inspection runs opening conference, walkaround, closing conference, citations. Both you and an employee representative may walk along. Employees can file confidential complaints, can refuse imminently dangerous work after asking you to fix it first, and are protected from retaliation.

Penalties come from Michigan statute, not the federal schedule. Serious and other-than-serious violations run up to seven thousand dollars each. Willful or repeat violations run up to seventy thousand, with a five thousand dollar minimum on willful. A willful violation that kills a worker is a felony. If an answer choice shows the federal sixteen thousand dollar figure, it's a trap. Michigan is seven and seventy.

Reporting and recordkeeping. A fatality must be reported to MIOSHA within eight hours of learning of it. An in-patient hospitalization, an amputation, or the loss of an eye must be reported within twenty four hours. Eight for a death, twenty four for the rest, never forty eight. Recordkeeping uses three forms: the three hundred log, the three hundred A annual summary, posted from February first through April thirtieth, and the three oh one incident report. Employers with ten or fewer employees are exempt from the routine logs, but nobody is ever exempt from the eight hour and twenty four hour reports.

One neighbor topic that rides along with safety: workers' compensation. A Michigan employer needs coverage with one or more employees working thirty five plus hours a week for thirteen or more weeks, or three or more employees at any one time. And if your subcontractor has no coverage and his worker gets hurt on your job, the general contractor can be on the hook. Verify every sub's certificate.
Time for the rapid-fire recap. Say these with me.
Fall protection: six feet. Scaffold guardrail: ten feet. Guardrail height: forty two inches, plus or minus three. Max free fall: six feet. Anchorage: five thousand pounds.
Ladders: four to one angle. Three feet above the landing. Ladder near power lines: twenty feet. Equipment near power lines: ten feet.
Trenches: protective system at five feet. Ladder at four feet, sticking up three feet, within twenty five feet of travel. Spoil pile: two feet back. Competent person: ongoing, and after every rain.
Soil: Type A, three quarters to one, fifty three degrees. Type B, one to one, forty five degrees. Type C, one and a half to one, thirty four degrees. Disturbed soil is never Type A.
MISS DIG: three full working days.
Scaffolds: four times the load. Two by ten planking. Never climb cross braces.
Electrical: G F C I on every temporary one twenty volt receptacle, or an assured grounding program.
Silica: fifty limit, twenty five action. Noise: ninety in construction.
Reporting: fatality eight hours. Hospitalization, amputation, eye: twenty four hours. Summary posted February first to April thirtieth. Ten or fewer employees: exempt from logs, never from reports.
Penalties: seven thousand serious. Seventy thousand willful or repeat, five thousand minimum.
And the agency: L E O runs MIOSHA, MIOSHA covers public employees, and the General Duty Clause fills every gap.
That's the domain. Ten questions, all numbers, all yours.
